title: Discovering Your Genjokoan Talk 2
speaker: Myoki Raizelah Bayen
summary: Myoki Raizelah Bayen's talk emphasizes the importance of cultivating mindfulness and self-acceptance, particularly during times of challenge or limitation, to find liberation from attachment and conceptual thinking. By embracing imperfection and letting go of expectations, we can transcend our fixed sense of self and experience a deeper understanding of ourselves and the world. This is reflected in the Genjokoan, which encourages us to leap beyond dualistic thinking and instead embody both our ordinary human experience and our Buddha nature.

sentences.text: *An unsurpassed, penetrating and perfect dharma is rarely met with even in a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I now taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.*
Okay, testing.
Is there a little echo right now?
No.
Good.
Well, thanks for coming, everyone.
I feel so honored and also humbled.
Maybe some of you received this card in the mail.
I don't know if it went to everybody at Red Cedar or if it went to everybody who made a donation.
The calligraphy on the front, which Tim made (he does this every year), means Sun Face Buddha, Moon Face Buddha.
And there's a little koan inside.
*Great Master Ma was unwell.
The temple leader asked, "Teacher, how has your venerable health been in recent days?"
And Ma replied, "Sun Face Buddha, Moon Face Buddha."*
This spoke to me: practicing with sickness, practicing with health.
I didn't expect to be practicing with COVID during this practice period, during this time of practicing as shuso.
But what an incredible lesson it's been for me in listening to the body, because my energy is very unpredictable.
It comes and it goes.
I don't know from one day to the next really how much energy I'll have.
I want to believe that I'm on a trajectory and that tomorrow I'll have more energy than I did today and so on.
But actually, it's not like that.
So it's a practice of listening, taking time to take care of myself.
I'm a doer.
When I was sick, I've often just overrode my body and kept going: oh, I can do this.
But COVID is different.
I bet I'm probably preaching to the choir here.
I think I'm one of the last people, at least that I know, to have gotten COVID.
So many of you have been through this, and many of you, if not with COVID, have practiced with illness, have practiced with disabilities, have practiced with limitations.
I take my hat off to you, because it's very humbling.
Body has its own way.
So let's swim a little more in the waters of the Genjokoan.
I'll start at the beginning, reviewing those first four lines that we talked about last Monday, and then I'll read a few more lines and we'll see what's moved in us.
So, again, let the words wash over you, let yourself bathe in these waters.
*All things are Buddha Dharma.
There is delusion and realization, practice, birth and death.
And there are Buddhas and sentient beings.
As the myriad things are without an abiding self, there is no delusion, no realization, no Buddha, no sentient being, no birth and death.
The Buddha way is basically leaping clear of the many and the one.
Thus there are birth and death, delusion and realization, sentient beings and Buddhas.
Yet an attachment blossoms fall and an aversion weeds spread.
To carry yourself forward and experience myriad things is delusion.
That myriad things come forth and experience themselves is awakening.
Those who have great realization of delusion are Buddhas.
Those who are greatly deluded about realization are sentient beings.
Further, there are those who continue realizing beyond realization, who are in delusion throughout delusion.
When Buddhas are truly Buddhas, they do not necessarily notice that they are Buddhas.
However, they are actualized Buddhas who go on actualizing Buddha.*
I didn't put the link earlier to the Genjokoan into the chat box, but what I'm going to do right now is put what I just read into the chat box.
So it'll be right there.
When I was preparing to teach this class, I gave myself a couple of what I called creators retreats.

I went away to Lopez Island and just immersed myself and focused completely on the Genjokoan, leaving behind the distractions that I feel when I try to work at home, the pull that I feel to do other things.
I was looking through my notes from one of my weekends on Lopez Island, and I found a little poem that I wrote.
I didn't remember writing it when I found it.
I'm like, who wrote this?
Oh, that was me.
I thought I would share it with you.
*There are two.
The world of convention, concepts, beliefs, ideas about myself and other ruling the world.
This is my conditioned mind.
This is my small mind.
There's one here, the absolute.
There are no bounds, boundlessness.
In this world, no concepts, no ideas, no beliefs, interdependence, interpenetrating, dynamic, co-origination, no self and no other.
There's big mind.
Leap clear.
Big mind holds the small mind with kindness, with compassion, and a warm feeling.*
So I want to share a story with you.
I mentioned last week that I had a story from the December one day sitting, the Rohatsu sitting, that I wanted to share.
I ran out of time last week, but it's a story about this, I think.
I feel a little vulnerable sharing it.
It's a story about my inner experience at the sitting, and I went home and did some journal writing after the one day sitting, so I had very clear notes from which to draw in resharing this with you.
I went through a period about a month or two ago when I was dipping into some low moods, just mildly depressed moods.
I think it was partially in response to some of the inner material that was coming up in preparing to teach this class.
I was feeling my insecurities, my inadequacies, and I was feeling very pulled into actually believing them.
It was really pulling my mood down.
So when I was sitting at the sesshin, I was just sitting with feeling that mildly depressed mood.
I was noticing the insecurities and the inadequacies that had been plaguing me.
My childhood conditioning about not being good enough was really strongly coming up.

As I sat with those depressed feelings at the one day sitting and checked in with my body, I could feel my body round over in this contracted way, and there was a posture of fear that I could feel in my body.
I don't think that my parents physically beat me, although there was a wooden paddle next to the fireplace.
If my mother got angry at me, she would threaten to ask my father to spank me with the paddle when he came home.
I don't have a memory of being spanked by that paddle, but I have a memory of the fear.
When my mother became angry or frustrated, she would hold her hand up to threaten to hit me, but she would stop herself.
The way she would stop herself is she would bite her hand, and she would bite it really hard, and I could see her shaking with the pain.
It felt like an eternity.

So as I sat on my cushion in that December one day sitting, I could feel myself shrink away in this posture of fear: the fear of being myself, the fear of not being good enough, the fear of disappointing.
And it also happened on that one day sitting that I was the Kokuyo.
So here's the other part of the story.
We were doing a ritual for Rohatsu and there was a chant that the Kokuyo was meant to lead.
That was me.
It was a chant I had never done before, an alternative kind of chanting.
You know the kind of chanting that we do, the singsongy Metta Sutta chant where the voice goes up one third and then down one third?
Well, this was another chant like that, and I was really nervous about doing it because it was new to me.
I didn't have much time to practice, and so I knew I would make mistakes.
But something really unexpected happened.
Something emerged out of sitting in this posture of fear: the will and the strength to just be myself.
I just decided, I'm going to sing the Kokuyo part as if I know what I'm doing, even though I knew I would make mistakes.
I let myself belt it out, just express myself.
Unexpectedly, in doing so, the posture released from my body, the contraction softened, and my mood lifted and morphed into something different.
It was as if I was leaping clear.
Maybe you experienced this when you really fully let yourself be in the moment with what's right there for you.
It changes.
Maybe this is what Dogen was talking about when he said the Buddha way is basically leaping clear.
I don't know.

I know that when I show up completely in my delusion, accepting it, accepting both the Moon Face and the Sun Face Buddha (so hard, right, because we all have preferences, I have strong preferences), I just accept it.
When I observe it with compassion, when the small mind is held by the big mind (Suzuki Roshi's terms, small mind, big mind), maybe this is actualizing the fundamental point.
These are questions.
**Participant:** So, I'm sorry I'm interrupting.
**Myoki Raizelah Bayen:** It's okay.
**Participant:** But I just want to say that it was really wonderful, and I was there and I could distinctly feel a shift when we actually did it.
I was just like, wow, sounded so great.
Yeah.
Anyway, great story.

**Myoki Raizelah Bayen:** I remember, Desiree, your supportive words after the ritual, because when I went into the ritual knowing that I was going to make mistakes, I thought, well, no one will know except Desiree and Tim will know.
But anyway, I so appreciated your supportive words.
Let's move forward.
The next line of the Genjokoan:
*To carry yourself forward and experience myriad things is delusion.
That myriad things come forth and experience themselves is awakening.*
Isn't life a mystery?
Truly beyond our knowing.
I have the feeling that I'm moving forward in my life making choices, right, choosing this direction or that direction in my work, choosing to practice, then choosing my husband.
But really, who is choosing?
How is this happening?
There's a feeling that I am choosing at the same time that life is choosing me.
So really, how did I get here, sitting right here with all of you in this Zoom room, talking about the Genjokoan?
I just want to tell you a little bit about my life, because it brings nothing but questions up for me.
Some of you know I teach continuing education to massage therapists.
By the grace of Buddha I seem to have been given the gift of teaching.
I never made a conscious choice to become a teacher.
I never set that as a goal for myself, nor did I ever know that would be a path that I walked.
Early in my career as a body worker I was invited to TA, to be a teaching assistant, at a couple of acupressure classes.
To my surprise, I discovered that I loved teaching, and that love just drew me in.
So I applied to teach at this [unclear: "basketball"] massage school, where I was living in California.
When I first started to teach there I was given one class a year, and by the time I left I was teaching eight classes a year.
I don't know how that happened.
In 2015 the director of that massage school sold the school.
And I moved on.
I was working at the time as a lead massage therapist in an Eastern-influenced day spa.
You might say it was a Zen-influenced day spa.
The owner was a Zen practitioner, and he had hired our old friend Steve Stuckey.
Maybe some of you knew of him.
He was a former abbot at Green Gulch Zen Center, a teacher in the Bay Area.
I had the privilege of sitting with him at times.
For a while before he became abbot at Green Gulch he was living in San Rafael, and he had converted his garage into a zendo.
I had the honor, the privilege, of sitting in that zendo, and that's in fact where I did my yoga teacher training.
Anyway, what Steve Stuckey did for a living when he wasn't at Green Gulch was design Japanese Zen meditation gardens, and he designed a beautiful garden for this day spa that I was working at.
It was meant to be a place where the spa guests could go and relax and reflect.
It was a quiet place.
I remember my first time sitting there, and just as my love of teaching drew me in, this garden drew me in, and some part of me said yes.
So when I was promoted from lead massage therapist to massage supervisor and then spa services manager, I continued to say yes, even though managing wasn't actually what I wanted to do.
That wasn't really my path.
I didn't ever feel like a manager even though I was one for 10 years.
In my heart of hearts, I was a teacher.
I really wanted to be teaching.
So I left that day spa and I opened my massage continuing education school, Open Pathways, which is what I currently do.
But when I look back on my life, it's like, what prompted those choices?
Was it really my choice?
Yes, it's true, I wasn't really happy as a spa manager.
I grew and I learned a lot in that role.
It was completely valuable, and I'm so glad that I did it.
But for part of that time, there was a spa director working over me who was really mean.
I remember one day on my way to work just pulling over, the car pulling over to the side of the road.
I just had to cry because she was so mean to me.
So there was suffering also woven into that experience of spa management.
It was as if I needed that particular flavor of suffering to fuel a change, to have the energy to say, it's time to move on and do something different.
But really, who made that choice?
And there's my Zen practice.
I tried to leave Zen.
I lived at Green Gulch when I was in my 20s, and I left formal practice because I wanted a practice that incorporated more of a psychological approach.
I practiced with a different spiritual work school for many years.
Then there was a day, about 20 years after my stay at Green Gulch, when I was in my early 40s.
I had two young children.
I was working, seeing massage clients, teaching massage classes, teaching yoga classes.
I was stretched really thin.
My ex-husband, at that time, said, "I want you to take a day off.
Just do something good for yourself.
A day off from being a mother, from work."
And for those of you who have been parents, a day off from parenting when you have two little kids, wow, that doesn't really happen.
So I thought, what am I going to do?
Day off?
Oh, I think I'll go do a one day sitting at Spirit Rock.
It was kind of an arbitrary choice.
I didn't even know who was leading the sitting.
I saw the title of the sitting, "For the One Who Is Not Busy," and I thought, oh, that's a good one for me.
But guess who was leading the sitting?
Someone I knew from my Green Gulch days 20 years earlier.
We recognized each other, and I picked up his brochure about Every Day Zen on my way out.
I went to the next one day sitting with Every Day Zen, and I felt immediately at home.
I was completely drawn in.
This was where I knew I needed to be.
And it was a complete accident.
I wasn't looking to return to Zen practice.
I wasn't looking to reconnect with Norman.
A similar accident happened in relationship to Tim.
We actually met when we were in our early 20s at Green Gulch, and we had a brief relationship at that time.
We were young hippies sneaking around, having a good time together.
But I was also really scared of intimacy.
So pretty quick, sadly, regretfully, I dumped him.
The Raizelah of her early 20s dumped him.
I can't actually believe I did that now, but at the time I couldn't do anything else.
We went our separate ways.
We forgot about each other.
We each got married to different people.
We had our families.
We didn't see each other for many years.
But when we reconnected in 2020, we discovered that those seeds of love had been tended to by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas at Green Gulch, and that that love was just waiting for us.
So when we met again, it was clear that we were going to make a life together.
It was as if our love found us as we found each other.
Life is a mystery, truly.
*To carry oneself forward and experience myriad things is delusion.
That myriad things come forth and experience themselves is awakening.*
So what I'm trying to say is my life was just a sequence of well-timed accidents over and over again, myriad things coming forth, drawing me in, inviting me into what I take to be my life.
But really, whose life is it?
*To carry yourself forward and experience myriad things is delusion.* The idea that I carry myself forward assumes duality, that I make a choice, right?
There's I and then there's the choice.
There's a built-in duality there.
This is the world of convention.
This is the world we live in, our relative existence.
But it's only a part of who we are.

Right in the beginning of the Genjokoan, there's both the relative, the two, and the one, the absolute: *that myriad things come forth and experience themselves is awakening.* We are a single wave in this vast ocean of being.
This ocean is alive, it's moving, it's flowing, it has tides that pull us in, that pull us out.
The flow of this immeasurable body of water carries us through this life.
We're not doing it alone.
We are profoundly interconnected with all the other waves.
So in a way we have no choice and we have choice.
Dogen is talking about both the relative and the relative, the dualistic dimension and the boundless dimension.
One doesn't exclude the other.
We're living in the middle of this dynamic relationship between the relative and the absolute, simultaneously expressed through us.
We are choosing and we are being chosen.
Okumura, right here, says:
*It is not I who practice, but rather Buddha carries out Buddha's practice through me.
In our Zazen practice and in our daily activity of bodhisattva practice, it is not a matter of individual acts based on individual willpower or effort.
It is rather the myriad dharmas or all beings that carry out practice through our individual bodies and minds.*
I'm going to say that again.
It's the myriad dharmas, or rather all beings, that carry out practice through our individual bodies and minds, and that carry out our life.
I mean, practice is life.
So I want to give you a chance to explore this in a very personal way.
I'm going to invite Ken to make groups of two.
In your dyad, just think about these questions.
What is your feeling for how you got here?
Do you feel in your life that you tend to push yourself upstream?
Or do you allow yourself to be pulled by the currents in this direction or that, drawn in?
What's your relationship to control?
I like to believe I'm in control.
Letting go to the life stream or current involves some faith or some trust.
Is that hard for you?
For me it is.
Maybe it's hard in some areas of your life, but not in others.
So when we're in the dyads, you're going to have eight minutes to discuss this, and I'll say those questions again.
I'll broadcast them also.
You're going to have eight minutes to discuss this in the context of your life.
And the other person is there providing a container, practicing active listening.
No need to respond.
No need to be in dialogue while each person does their monologue.
There's no need to help or fix or advise.
Just stay present.
That's your job as the listener: to fully show up.
To fully show up, my translation of Koan.
Then after the first person talks for eight minutes, the other person gets eight minutes to talk.
After both people get a chance to be fully listened to, you'll have four minutes for some dialoguing.
I will put in the broadcast when it's time to switch partners and when it's time to dialogue.
So let me say this one more time.
Actually, let me put it in the chat box and read it.
Oops, there's a typo here.
Okay.
I forgot to press send when I put in the Genjokoan lines earlier.
Here is the topic for the dialogue, the monologue.
What is your feeling for how you got here?
Do you feel in your life that you tend to push upstream, or do you allow yourself to be pulled by the currents in this direction or that?
What is your relationship to control?
Letting go to life's stream or current involves some faith or trust.
Is it hard for you?
Maybe it's hard in some areas of life, but not in others.
So just talk about this.
After you make the breakout rooms, Ken, I'm also going to broadcast these questions.
I'm going to fix my typo.
There may be one room with three people.
Okay, so just due to numbers, it's allowing me to do two to three participants per room.
You could maybe move people around.
Do you see that feature?
Yes.
And if it still works out that there's a group of three, then the threesome should just each do a monologue of six minutes instead of eight.
Six times three is 18.
The threesome probably won't have time to have that conversation at the end, as the twosomes will.
When I broadcast that it's time to change partners, I'll do it for the twosomes since almost everybody will be in a twosome.
I'll just ask that that one threesome assign a timer who times people six minutes each.
Okay, so go ahead and invite people to the rooms, Ken, if you're ready for that.
I'm going to have to assign manually.
This may take a second.
I apologize.
**Participant:** Oh, okay.
Yeah.
Thank you for your personal sharing and stories.
They are deeply revealing of Genjokoan and yourself.
Appreciate it.
**Myoki Raizelah Bayen:** Thanks, Sam.
Not all of you know Sam.
Can I say something?
He lives in California, but his mother, Cindy Morninglight, was a friend, not just a friend of mine at Everyday Zen.
She and I sewed our rakusus together and we received Jukai together.
So whenever I see Sam, I think of his mama, who blessedly passed on a few years ago.
Bye, everybody.
So there are a couple more lines I want to speak to from the Genjokoan, and then I do want to give you all a chance to share what's been moved in you.
I think I'm going to save that for the end.
You can hold your thoughts and feelings, because there's lots.
There's lots of Genjokoan and only seven weeks.
*Those who have great realization of delusion are Buddhas and those who are greatly deluded about realization are sentient beings.*
This is the next line.

*Those who have great realization of delusion are Buddhas and those who are greatly deluded about realization are sentient beings.* So here Dogen is talking again about this interpenetration of both the relative and the absolute, delusion and enlightenment.
Nishiari is one of the commentators in this book.
He's the third, the [unclear: "back"] commentator.
This is a quote from him.
He says:
*Delusion is Genjokoan.
Enlightenment is Genjokoan.
It is not different dharmas are seen as delusion or enlightenment, but that we are deluded and enlightened about the same things.*
So when we face delusion, we say sentient beings, and when we face enlightenment, we say all Buddhas.
But ultimately, they're the same thing.
So for me, the hard part is not getting caught by either one.
I find myself clinging to this idea about myself or grasping for liberation from that idea about myself, clinging and pushing away, all at the same time.
And of course, this is why I need practice.
We need practice to come back to my body, to settle right here, to breathe and to bring awareness to my clinging and my grasping, to my attachments and aversions.
And then maybe by Buddha's grace, I can let go.
Sometimes it happens.
It's usually, never actually, my choice.
But how do we hold them both, this dynamic, interpenetrating relationship between our constantly arising delusion and our enlightenment?
And do we even need to?
It just is, right?
Next line:
*And even though we are living within this universal reality, we are still deluded, deluded, individual karmic selves.*
We're completely deluded.
I'm completely deluded every moment.
And we're completely enlightened.
Suzuki Roshi is often quoted as saying, you're perfect the way you are, and you could use a little improvement, right?
You're perfectly enlightened and you could use a little improvement.
We have always been and will always be both deluded and enlightened.
And so we always have and will forever continue to discover these endless layers of delusion and the endless expression of our enlightenment.
Then Dogen writes in the Genjokoan:
*When Buddhas are truly Buddhas, they do not necessarily notice that they are Buddhas.
However, they are actualized Buddhas and go on actualizing Buddhas.*
In Norman Fischer's fourth talk about the Genjokoan, he reminds us that if we even try to talk about enlightenment or Buddhahood, we're already removed from it.
This is the nature of language.
You can't actually talk about it because as soon as you use words to describe it, there's already some separation.
You're already trapped in the conceptual mind, which is the only way our mind knows how to work in this relative world.
As soon as you talk about being a Buddha or enlightened, there's an I and there's a self and an other, the idea that you're talking about.
So if Buddhas recognize themselves as Buddhas, they're trapped in dualism, the polarity of self and other.
They're already separate.
How do you talk about it?
It's not really possible.
If we enter the conceptual mind of separation and duality, we've left behind the unity of being.
Okumura says we cannot judge whether we are Buddhas or not because true reality is beyond such judgment.
There is no independent I in "I become a Buddha."
When we sit zazen, letting go of thoughts, placing ourselves on the ground of reality, our practice manifests Buddha.
These are my words now: our life manifests Buddha.
Buddha is manifesting [unclear: "Hammer her, their self"] through us.
Okumura goes on to say, so quoting Okumura again:
*When we sit in the upright posture, keeping the eyes open, breathing through the nose and letting go of thoughts, reality manifests itself.
This is Genjokoan, the actualization of reality.*
That's it.
That's Genjokoan.
When we practice, reality manifests itself.
Dogen has coined a term for this.
He calls it practice enlightenment, all one word, practice enlightenment.
Suzuki Roshi says it in slightly different words:
*When you sit zazen, you're independent from various beings and you're related to various beings.
And when you have perfect composure in your practice, you include everything.
No preferences.
You are not just you.
You are the whole world or the whole cosmos and you're Buddha.
So when you sit, you're an ordinary human being and you're Buddha.*
So here Suzuki Roshi refers to perfect composure.
He says when you have perfect composure in practice, you include everything.
I feel like he's echoing Dogen's words, *in attachment blossoms fall and in aversions weeds spread.* He's saying don't have preferences.
He says again, you are not just you.
You're the whole world or the whole cosmos and you're Buddha.
So when you sit, you're an ordinary human being and you're Buddha.
You're everything all together: this interpenetrating ordinary person, snared by dualistic views, and you're Buddha, the boundless dimension of the absolute.
And this completely dynamic, interpenetrating, co-arising relationship.
I think you're starting to see now the theme of the Genjokoan.
Dogen basically says the same thing in many different words.
The first three lines of the Genjokoan are repeated using different metaphors and different stories as we move through the Genjokoan.
But coming back always to this idea that we're both ordinary human beings and we're Buddhas.
And then in some way, the Buddha way is to leap clear of both: the two and the one.
Not two, not one.
Both and neither.
Thanks for listening.
I really want to give all of you a chance to talk and share what moved you in the dyad.

I'm also really interested, and maybe this is a little bit selfish, because the sentence that has most pulled my attention is the third line: *The Buddha way is leaping clear of the many and the one.* This idea of leaping clear.
What is leaping clear look like in your life?
I'm going to pause the recording.
